paragraphs: Deep learning often needs more labeled examples than are practical to collect. A common workaround creates additional examples by changing the geometry or appearance of existing ones. This paper questions whether those transformations reliably describe how new examples arise and develops a Bayesian alternative that learns how to generate annotated data from the training set.

The central move is to treat additional training examples as missing variables. Their values are generated according to a learned distribution, making augmentation part of the statistical learning problem. The authors introduce generalized Monte Carlo expectation maximization for this purpose and present an extension of a generative adversarial network as one possible implementation.

On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, the proposed method produces better classification results than the transformation-based augmentation approach described in the abstract and similar GAN models. These findings support learned augmentation in the evaluated settings: the generated examples help classification, connecting the quality of augmentation to the eventual task rather than only to the generation process.
neurips-2017-a-bayesian-data-augmentatio.tldr: A Bayesian approach learns to generate labeled training examples and improves classification over the compared augmentation methods on three datasets.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs a matrix from its observed entries. Many theories assume those entries are sampled uniformly at random, but actual missingness can depend on the unseen values and follow an irregular, deterministic pattern. This paper develops a theoretical framework intended to cover a broader range of observation patterns.

Its main ingredient is the isomeric condition, which the authors prove is weaker than the uniform-sampling assumption. They argue that it can hold even with irregularly placed missing entries. Using this condition, they establish results for missing-data recovery and matrix completion, expanding the circumstances in which recovery can be analyzed.

A central result shows that exact target-recovering solutions occur among the critical points of commonly used nonconvex programs. This establishes their presence in the optimization landscape; it does not establish that every critical point recovers the target. The theory indicates that nonconvex formulations have the potential to operate under substantially weaker conditions than those used in earlier analyses, while offering a more general setup for nonuniform observations.
neurips-2017-a-new-theory-for-matrix-com.tldr: A weaker condition on observed entries broadens matrix-completion theory and shows that exact solutions can be critical points of nonconvex formulations.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms can converge quickly when a problem satisfies an error bound, a property that relates progress in the objective to proximity to a solution. Quadratic error bounds generalize strong convexity and apply to a broad family of machine learning problems. They have supported linear convergence results for methods including stochastic variance reduced gradient, or SVRG.

The practical obstacle is that these algorithms can require a growth parameter from the error bound. That quantity is generally unknown and difficult to estimate exactly. Choosing it heuristically leaves a gap between an algorithm's theoretical guarantees and the version that can actually be run.

The paper introduces SVRG variants that search for this parameter during optimization. Their convergence rates are almost the same as those available when the parameter is known, preserving most of the theoretical benefit while removing the need to supply its exact value beforehand. The authors also analyze SVRG under Hölderian error bounds, extending the investigation beyond the quadratic case.
neurips-2017-adaptive-svrg-methods-under.tldr: Adaptive SVRG methods search for an unknown error-bound parameter during optimization while retaining nearly the convergence rate available when it is known.

paragraphs: Experimental design involves choosing measurements that will make an estimate informative. Greedy methods build a design through successive choices, but standard performance guarantees rely on mathematical structure that some important objectives lack. This paper studies A-optimal and E-optimal design, which concern mean-square estimation error and the largest eigenvalue of the estimation error covariance matrix.

Neither of these objectives is supermodular, so the usual guarantee cannot be applied directly. The authors instead measure approximate supermodularity and use it to derive finite, worst-case bounds on how far greedy solutions can fall short. This makes the analysis useful without requiring the objectives to possess the exact structural property.

The bounds show that the objectives behave increasingly like supermodular functions as experimental signal-to-noise ratios decrease. In that regime, the greedy designs approach a 1−1/e optimality guarantee. The result helps explain why greedy experimental design can work well empirically despite failing the standard supermodularity test. This concerns the quality of selection relative to the optimum, not a claim that noisier measurements provide more information.
neurips-2017-approximate-supermodularity.tldr: Approximate supermodularity gives worst-case guarantees for greedy A- and E-optimal experimental designs, with stronger guarantees as signal-to-noise ratios decrease.

paragraphs: Generative dialog models can compose responses, but training them to match human answers through maximum likelihood often produces generic replies. Discriminative models can rank candidate human responses more effectively and favor greater diversity and informativeness, yet candidate ranking does not itself provide free-form conversation. This paper transfers knowledge from a discriminative model into a generative visual dialog model.

The generator receives a perceptual training loss from the discriminative model for a sampled response. This loss is not adversarial. Because sampling discrete words obstructs ordinary differentiation, the authors combine Gumbel-Softmax samplers with a straight-through gradient estimator, allowing training signals to pass through the generated sequence.

The framework also strengthens visual dialog encoding and uses answer self-attention with a metric learning loss to help the discriminative model capture semantic similarities. The resulting model improves over the reported state of the art on VisDial by 2.67% on recall@10. The finding supports using learned response judgments to improve a model that retains the ability to generate answers.
neurips-2017-best-of-both-worlds-transfe.tldr: A visual dialog generator learns from a discriminative model through a differentiable perceptual loss, improving reported VisDial performance.

paragraphs: Asynchronous optimization lets multiple processor cores work without waiting for every update to finish together. Such methods have been successful for large learning problems, but support for nonsmooth objectives has lagged behind. That gap matters for applications involving penalties or constraints, including Lasso, group Lasso, and constrained empirical risk minimization.

The paper introduces ProxASAGA, a fully asynchronous sparse method inspired by SAGA, an incremental gradient algorithm that reduces variance. Its design extends this approach to composite objectives with a proximal term. The authors describe the method as easy to implement and analyze how its parallel execution compares with a sequential version.

The theoretical linear speedup depends on assumptions about gradient sparsity and block separability of the proximal term. It therefore applies to problems with the required structure. Experiments on several large nonsmooth problems show substantial improvements over the compared state of the art, including practical speedups of up to twelve times on a twenty-core machine. These results demonstrate useful parallel gains without claiming perfect scaling in every setting.
neurips-2017-breaking-the-nonsmooth-barr.tldr: ProxASAGA brings asynchronous parallel optimization to nonsmooth problems, with conditional linear-speedup guarantees and measured speedups of up to twelve times.

paragraphs: When a model learns tasks one after another, training on the latest task can damage what it learned earlier. Replaying all past training data can alleviate this catastrophic forgetting, but storing and accessing those examples may be impractical. This paper proposes Deep Generative Replay as a way to revisit earlier tasks through generated data.

The framework pairs two cooperating models: a generator and a solver. The generator supplies samples representing previous tasks, while the solver learns to perform tasks. During training on a new task, generated samples from earlier tasks are interleaved with new examples, allowing the training process to include both past and present experience.

The approach is inspired by the generative role attributed to the hippocampus as a short-term memory system. Its practical contribution is an architecture that makes replay possible through the two learned models when access to original past data is limited. The authors test it in several sequential image-classification settings, examining this mechanism in the kind of task sequence where forgetting arises.
neurips-2017-continual-learning-with-dee.tldr: Deep Generative Replay mixes generated examples of earlier tasks with new data to address forgetting during sequential learning.

paragraphs: Functional alignment makes fMRI representations from different subjects more comparable. This becomes difficult when the relationships are nonlinear, brain regions contain many dimensions, and datasets include many people. Deep Hyperalignment addresses these demands through a regularized deep extension of hyperalignment designed to scale to larger datasets.

The method uses a parametric approach rather than restricting alignment to a fixed kernel function. Its optimization combines rank-m singular value decomposition with stochastic gradient descent. These choices provide the computational basis for handling high-dimensional regions of interest and many subjects while allowing nonlinear relationships in the alignment.

A useful operational property is that alignment for a new subject does not require the original training data. The learned parametric approach can therefore be applied without retaining that data for this step. Experiments on multi-subject fMRI analysis report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art hyperalignment algorithms. Together, the results support the method's proposed combination of flexible alignment and computational practicality in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2017-deep-hyperalignment-087454b.tldr: Deep Hyperalignment learns scalable nonlinear fMRI alignment and can align a new subject without using the original training data.

paragraphs: Learning logical rules for a knowledge base involves two coupled decisions: what form a rule should take and what numerical parameters it should have. The first is a discrete structural choice, while the second lies in a continuous space. This mismatch makes it difficult to learn both parts within a single optimization process.

Neural Logic Programming combines rule structure and parameter learning in an end-to-end differentiable framework. It builds on the idea, used in TensorLog, that logical inference can be expressed as a sequence of differentiable operations. A neural controller learns how to compose these operations, connecting the construction of reasoning procedures to trainable numerical components.

The contribution is therefore a way to learn probabilistic first-order rules while keeping the overall model differentiable. Empirical results show improvements over prior work on multiple knowledge-base benchmarks, including Freebase and WikiMovies. These findings support the usefulness of the combined learning approach for the evaluated reasoning tasks, where deciding how to assemble a rule is part of learning.
neurips-2017-differentiable-learning-of-.tldr: Neural Logic Programming jointly learns logical-rule structures and parameters through differentiable operations controlled by a neural model.

paragraphs: Learning several reinforcement-learning tasks together could reduce the experience needed for each one. Directly sharing neural-network parameters can undermine that benefit, however: updates from different tasks may conflict, and differences in rewards can let one task dominate. Distral introduces a shared behavioral reference to organize transfer across tasks.

Each task has its own policy, trained to solve that task while remaining close to a shared distilled policy. The shared policy is updated through distillation to represent a centroid of the individual policies. A joint objective governs both directions of learning, so task-specific behavior contributes to the common policy and the common policy guides each task.

This arrangement gives the tasks a common source of behavior while preserving their separate learning objectives. In complex three-dimensional environments, the authors report efficient transfer and better performance than several related methods. They also find the training process more stable and robust. These empirical findings address the interference and instability that motivated the approach to joint training.
neurips-2017-distral-robust-multitask-re.tldr: Distral transfers behavior through a shared distilled policy, improving multitask reinforcement learning in the evaluated three-dimensional environments.

paragraphs: Kernel methods offer a principled way to learn nonlinear relationships and have strong statistical foundations. Their basic implementations can nevertheless demand too much computation and memory for large datasets. FALKON addresses this gap between statistical appeal and practical scale with an algorithm designed to process millions of data points.

The method combines stochastic subsampling, iterative solvers, and preconditioning. Together, these algorithmic ingredients reduce the resources needed to carry out kernel learning. The theoretical analysis shows that optimal statistical accuracy can be achieved with essentially linear memory in the number of examples, n, and a running time proportional to n times the square root of n.

The significance is that computational savings are accompanied by an accuracy guarantee. The authors also evaluate FALKON extensively on large datasets and report that it outperforms previous state-of-the-art solutions using parallel or distributed architectures, even when FALKON runs on one machine. This supports its practicality in the tested settings alongside the theoretical scaling result.
neurips-2017-falkon-an-optimal-large-sca.tldr: FALKON scales kernel learning to millions of examples while achieving optimal statistical accuracy with essentially linear memory.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks learn complex distributions, but stable training depends in part on how differences between distributions are measured. Fisher GAN introduces a formulation within the integral probability metric framework. In this setting, a critic supplies the function used to distinguish the distributions during training.

The distinguishing feature is a data-dependent constraint on the critic's second-order moments. This controls the critic through its behavior on data rather than through a data-independent restriction such as clipping its weights. The authors analyze the resulting Fisher metric theoretically and develop an optimization algorithm based on an augmented Lagrangian.

The paper reports stable, time-efficient training without compromising the critic's capacity or requiring weight clipping. It evaluates these claims through both image generation and semi-supervised classification. These applications connect the mathematical constraint to practical learning behavior: the proposed control of the critic is useful not only for producing samples but also in a setting that combines labeled and unlabeled data for classification.
neurips-2017-fisher-gan-31c7e79670.tldr: Fisher GAN uses a data-dependent moment constraint on its critic to support stable, efficient training without weight clipping.

paragraphs: Constraints can make estimation in generalized linear models difficult. Penalizing the likelihood is one way to incorporate them, but familiar penalties such as the lasso can shrink estimates severely. This paper investigates a different construction: penalizing the squared distance between a candidate estimate and a set representing the desired constraint.

This makes the constraint set itself the reference for the penalty. The authors describe distance penalties as more flexible than algebraic and regularization penalties and as avoiding the shrinkage drawback. To optimize the resulting objectives, they use majorization-minimization, a framework that proceeds through objectives designed to make the optimization more manageable.

The resulting algorithms admit acceleration and have global convergence guarantees. The paper applies them to shape constraints, sparse regression, and matrix regression with rank restrictions, using both synthetic and real data. Strong empirical performance includes cases with nonconvex constraints. These results support distance penalization as a common approach to several kinds of structured estimation, while the optimization guarantees should not be confused with a blanket claim of globally optimal nonconvex solutions.
neurips-2017-generalized-linear-model-re.tldr: Squared-distance penalties provide a flexible approach to constrained generalized linear models, with convergent optimization algorithms and strong reported empirical performance.

paragraphs: Some datasets describe objects only through relative similarity judgments: one object resembles a second more than a third. These triplets give comparative information without supplying ordinary feature vectors or exact numerical distances. The paper asks how such evidence can support the use of kernel methods on the objects.

The authors propose two constructions of kernel functions from similarity triplets. Earlier approaches described in the abstract first seek a low-dimensional Euclidean embedding that reflects the comparisons. Here, the goal is to define kernels corresponding to high-dimensional embeddings, making a different representation of the same type of evidence available for learning.

The practical contribution is the connection to the broader kernel-method framework. Once a kernel is defined on the dataset, it can be used by any kernel method. Thus, the triplet information becomes an input to an existing family of learning techniques rather than serving only to arrange objects in a low-dimensional space. The stated contribution concerns these constructions and their downstream applicability, without asserting a particular empirical accuracy gain.
neurips-2017-kernel-functions-based-on-t.tldr: Two kernel constructions turn relative similarity triplets into representations usable by kernel methods.

paragraphs: A conventional image network learns filters for perspective images, whereas a full spherical image cannot be flattened without substantial distortion. Repeatedly projecting a sphere onto local tangent planes can preserve accuracy, but it is computationally expensive. This paper learns a spherical convolutional network that processes the equirectangular representation of a 360-degree image directly.

The network learns to reproduce the outputs of planar filters while accounting for distortion that varies across the sphere. This allows it to reuse the capabilities of pretrained perspective-image networks, along with the benefits of the labeled data used to train them. The approach targets efficient feature extraction for both images and video.

Evaluation examines agreement with CNN outputs and the application of a state-of-the-art planar object detector to spherical imagery. The authors report the most accurate results among the evaluated alternatives and computation savings of orders of magnitude relative to exact reprojection. These findings support learned spherical processing as a practical route to using existing image-network capabilities on 360-degree data.
neurips-2017-learning-spherical-convolut.tldr: A learned spherical network adapts pretrained planar CNNs to 360-degree imagery while greatly reducing computation relative to exact reprojection.

paragraphs: A precision matrix is the inverse of a covariance matrix. Under a multivariate normal assumption, its pattern of zero and nonzero entries describes conditional independence relationships among variables. Estimating this matrix accurately is therefore useful for understanding multivariate structure. This paper establishes minimax estimation bounds for banded precision matrices under spectral-norm error.

The key construction estimates small blocks of the precision matrix by inverting slightly wider blocks of the empirical covariance matrix along its diagonal. The authors show that this produces estimates with very little noise. This local block strategy supplies the central insight needed to sharpen the theoretical bounds.

The resulting minimax rate matches the rate for estimating banded covariance matrices and substantially improves the existing precision-matrix bounds. Minimax analysis concerns the best achievable worst-case error over the matrix class under study, so the result characterizes the statistical difficulty of the estimation problem. Experiments complement the theory by demonstrating the sharpness of the bounds, supporting their relevance to observed estimation behavior.
neurips-2017-minimax-estimation-of-banda.tldr: A local block-inversion analysis yields sharper minimax bounds for banded precision matrices, matching the rate for banded covariance estimation.

paragraphs: Randomly weighted neural networks matter for understanding initialization and for studying random-feature and kernel methods. Although their construction involves random matrices, nonlinear activation functions make standard random-matrix results difficult to apply directly. This paper shows how typical pointwise nonlinearities can be incorporated into the moments method, an established proof technique in random matrix theory.

The analysis studies the Gram matrix YᵀY, where Y = f(WX), W contains random weights, X contains random data, and f applies an activation to each entry. The authors derive an explicit representation of the trace of its resolvent, a mathematical quantity that determines the limiting distribution of the matrix's eigenvalues.

They use this result to calculate asymptotic performance on a memorization task for single-layer random-feature methods and to analyze covariance eigenvalues as data passes through a neural network. The analysis also identifies a class of activation functions with favorable properties. The contribution connects nonlinear network computations to spectral tools that were previously difficult to use in this setting.
neurips-2017-nonlinear-random-matrix-the.tldr: The paper incorporates neural-network nonlinearities into random matrix analysis to study random features and covariance spectra.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weak learners into a stronger predictor. The theoretical work described in this paper had addressed multiclass classification in batch learning and online learning for binary classification, leaving their intersection unresolved. The authors develop a framework for boosting when learning is online and predictions can belong to more than two classes.

Their starting point is a weak-learning condition suited to this combined setting. Defining and justifying that condition establishes what the component learners must provide for the boosting analysis to work. It leads to an optimal algorithm in a specific sense: the algorithm needs the minimum number of weak learners to reach a given accuracy.

The paper also proposes an adaptive algorithm that is near optimal and performs strongly on real data. The abstract attributes its practical performance to adaptivity. Together, the algorithms connect a theoretical requirement on weak learners to both an optimal learner-count result and an adaptive alternative, giving the online multiclass setting its own boosting foundations.
neurips-2017-online-multiclass-boosting-.tldr: A weak-learning condition for online multiclass boosting supports an optimal learner-count algorithm and a near-optimal adaptive alternative.

paragraphs: Bayesian generalized linear models offer uncertainty estimates and a way to include prior information, but inference can become expensive on large datasets. Existing approximations can face a tradeoff between scalability and guarantees about their quality. PASS-GLM addresses this through polynomial approximate sufficient statistics: compact summaries designed to support approximate inference.

The resulting method has a simple algorithm and straightforward streaming and distributed extensions. The abstract states that these extensions do not compound error across computations. The authors also give theoretical guarantees covering maximum a posteriori point estimates, the approximate posterior distribution, and posterior estimates of means and uncertainty.

Experiments focus on logistic regression using a quadratic approximation. They show competitive speed and accuracy against stochastic gradient descent, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and the Laplace approximation, including on an advertising dataset with forty million examples and twenty thousand covariates. The contribution links large-scale computation to guarantees on several inferential outputs, including uncertainty, rather than assessing scalability only through a single fitted parameter estimate.
neurips-2017-pass-glm-polynomial-approxi.tldr: PASS-GLM uses polynomial data summaries for scalable Bayesian inference with guarantees on point estimates, posterior approximations, and uncertainty.

paragraphs: This paper studies neural networks as geometric transformations of coordinates on an underlying data manifold. The goal is to contribute to a formal theory of networks using Riemannian geometry, where a metric describes the geometry of that manifold. The analysis develops and proves results for feedforward networks from this perspective.

One result identifies residual networks as finite-difference approximations to dynamical systems governed by first-order differential equations. In this interpretation, learning a residual network amounts to learning equations that govern transformations of the data's coordinates. This provides a dynamical reading of the network's successive transformations.

A second result gives a closed-form expression for the underlying manifold's metric tensor by backpropagating coordinate representations learned by the network. The formal treatment expresses this through Lie group actions and geometric bundles. Toy experiments confirm parts of the proposed theory and provide intuition about how networks transform data. Their role is to illustrate and support portions of the geometric account, while the principal contributions are the theoretical relationships.
neurips-2017-principles-of-riemannian-ge.tldr: A geometric theory connects residual networks to differential equations and derives a manifold metric from learned coordinate transformations.

paragraphs: An online advertiser repeatedly chooses bids using information available before each auction, such as browser-cookie features. The objective is to maximize total utility over a fixed horizon while respecting a budget. This paper represents the side information as a d-dimensional vector and treats bid selection as a contextual bandit problem.

The formulation includes a knapsack constraint to represent the spending limit and a continuum of possible actions to represent bids. The authors develop upper-confidence-bound algorithms that combine confidence sets from linear contextual bandits with probabilistic bisection, a technique for finding roots when observations are stochastic.

Under assumptions on the unknown underlying distribution, they establish distribution-independent regret bounds of order d times the square root of the horizon T, up to logarithmic factors. The bounds apply when the budget is unlimited or grows linearly with T. These conditions are part of the guarantee: the result provides a controlled rate of regret growth for those budget regimes rather than for every possible spending limit.
neurips-2017-real-time-bidding-with-side.tldr: Contextual bandit algorithms provide bidding regret guarantees under distributional assumptions when budgets are unlimited or scale linearly with the horizon.

paragraphs: Some learning tasks benefit from repeatedly refining an interpretation, while others require tracking how information changes over time. This paper introduces a recurrent extension of Ladder networks to address both needs. Its structure is motivated by the inference processes needed in hierarchical latent-variable models, connecting recurrence to learning multiple levels of abstraction.

The architecture is tested on tasks involving temporal modeling and perceptual grouping. Reported results include near-optimal performance on video temporal modeling, competitive performance on music modeling, and improved grouping using higher-level information such as stochastic textures and motion cues. These applications examine different ways that iterative processing and temporal information can support learning.

The evaluation includes fully supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised tasks, so the architecture is investigated under different amounts of explicit teaching information. The findings suggest that recurrent Ladder networks provide useful principles for learning abstraction hierarchies, iterative inference, and temporal structure. That conclusion is supported by the reported variety of tasks rather than a claim that recurrence is optimal for every learning problem.
neurips-2017-recurrent-ladder-networks-2.tldr: Recurrent Ladder networks support iterative inference and temporal modeling across several tasks and supervision settings.

paragraphs: An agent learning from demonstrations is more likely to know what to do in situations resembling those its teacher showed. State Aware Imitation Learning, or SAIL, uses this observation directly. It aims to teach an agent both to remain in familiar states where it can act confidently and to recover when it moves away from them.

The mechanism is a learned gradient that favors states similar to the demonstrated states. A temporal-difference update rule learns this directional information. This supplements the policy's action choices with information about which states are more consistent with the demonstrations, making the agent's situation part of the imitation-learning strategy.

The theoretical analysis concerns a linear approximation of this gradient and gives guarantees similar to those of online temporal-difference learning. Separately, experiments show effective imitation learning in continuous domains using nonlinear function approximators for both the policy and the gradient estimate. Keeping these scopes distinct matters: the nonlinear empirical findings extend the demonstrated practical use beyond the specific approximation covered by the stated theory.
neurips-2017-state-aware-imitation-learn.tldr: SAIL learns a direction toward demonstrated states to help imitation-learning agents remain in familiar situations and recover from deviations.

paragraphs: Sequential data contains information that varies over different timescales. This paper uses that structure to learn separate, interpretable representations without supervision. It introduces a factorized hierarchical variational autoencoder whose graphical model explicitly distinguishes different groups of latent variables through sequence-dependent and sequence-independent prior distributions.

The design gives the model a structural basis for separating kinds of information that coexist in a sequence. On two speech corpora, qualitative experiments manipulate different latent-variable groups to transform either the speaker or the linguistic content. These demonstrations show that the learned variables can provide distinct controls over meaningful properties of speech.

Quantitative evaluations report better speaker verification than an i-vector baseline and reductions in speech-recognition word error rate of as much as 35% when training and testing conditions are mismatched. These findings connect interpretability to task utility: the representations support both controlled changes to speech and improvements in the evaluated applications. The largest reported error reduction belongs specifically to the mismatched train/test scenarios.
neurips-2017-unsupervised-learning-of-di.tldr: A hierarchical variational autoencoder separates speech factors without supervision and improves evaluated speaker-verification and mismatched speech-recognition tasks.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent optimizes an objective by updating individual coordinates. Cyclic methods follow a fixed order, while randomized methods choose coordinates randomly. Earlier convergence estimates suggested an advantage for randomization, but numerical experiments did not clearly establish that comparison. This paper investigates situations in which a deterministic update order has a theoretical advantage.

The authors provide examples and broader problem classes where cyclic coordinate descent, or descent with any deterministic order, converges faster than its randomized counterpart in an asymptotic worst-case sense. This establishes that the apparent ranking from earlier estimates does not describe all problem classes.

They also bound the size of the improvement and show that it depends on the chosen deterministic order. A further result characterizes the best order through combinatorial properties of the objective's Hessian matrix, linking scheduling decisions to the objective's structure. The contribution therefore goes beyond demonstrating that fixed orders can win: it analyzes how much they can help and what determines the most favorable ordering.
neurips-2017-when-cyclic-coordinate-desc.tldr: The paper identifies problem classes where deterministic coordinate descent is asymptotically faster than randomization and characterizes how update order affects the gain.
